definition: cause surprise or confusion; mix up or thwart
memoryTip: Con-found: throw into confusion — mix up or leave people stunned.
correctPassage: The experiment’s results continued to confound researchers who had predicted a simpler pattern.
wrongPassages: A careful chronology helped confound the sequence of events for the investigating panel.
She hoped the abstract would confound her thesis by restating each claim in plainer language.
New measurements confound the earlier study by reproducing its main findings almost exactly.

memoryTip: Dis + regard — drop your regard; treat it as if it doesn’t matter.
correctPassage: Critics accused the agency of disregard for the community’s documented concerns.
wrongPassages: Her disregard for the sources meant she checked every citation before the article went to press.
The board’s disregard for the proposal involved weeks of debate and a full public hearing.
Students showed disregard for the assignment by submitting detailed drafts well ahead of the deadline.

memoryTip: Like underlining a line — you underscore what matters most.
correctPassage: The new findings underscore the need for longer-term studies of the treatment.
wrongPassages: He underscored the conclusion by omitting it from the final presentation entirely.
The footnote underscored the claim by questioning every piece of supporting evidence.
Editors underscored the story’s importance by moving it to a less prominent section.

definition: conforming to traditional or established doctrine
memoryTip: Ortho = straight — by-the-book, traditional belief or method.
correctPassage: Her approach departed from orthodox methods that the field had relied on for decades.
wrongPassages: His orthodox redesign rejected every convention the profession still treated as standard.
Critics called the film orthodox for abandoning the genre’s familiar narrative structure.
She followed an orthodox training plan built only from experimental techniques no coach had tried.

definition: the highest point; peak of power or success
memoryTip: Highest point in the sky — and the peak of a career or empire.
correctPassage: The empire reached its zenith under the second emperor’s long and stable rule.
wrongPassages: The firm reached its zenith the year losses forced a major restructuring of the company.
At the zenith of the dig, crews finally exposed the lowest foundation stones of the fort.
Historians place the movement’s zenith in the obscure years before it gained any public following.
